To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

infants who are classified as being more easily frustrated are characterized by their parents and by their own behavior as less attentive, more active and more distressed to new stimuli, and they are more physiologically reactive than infants classified as less easily frustrated.

easily frustrated infants are more likely than less easily frustrated ones to be characterized by parents as more active and less attentive and are less able to regulate their attentional and physiological arousal when presented with novel situations.

infants who are easily frustrated use different emotion regulation strategies, are less attentive and more reactive physiogically, and have a different temperament than their less easily frustated counterparts.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the role of emotion in the development of temperament.
the development of emotion regulation in infants, with a focus on the role of temperament in the regulation of physiological reactivity.
the development of individual differences in temperament, particularly the construct of frustration.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
easily frustrated infants may be characterized by a unique cluster of characteristics that may have implications across a range of behavioral and physiological domains.
the easily frustrated infant is more reactive physiologcially, more easily distressed, and less able to use effective emotion regulation strategies.

frustration in infancy is a complex construct that is associated with a cluster of characteristics that may be related to other temperamental characteristics and may have implications for later behavioral and physiological functioning.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

infants who are more easily frustrated are less able to regulate their physiological reactivity and are more likely to use maladaptive emotion regulation strategies than less easily frustrated children.
infants classified as easily frustrated are more reactive physiologially and less able to self-regulate their physiological arousal than less easily frustrated counterparts.
easily frustrated infants are less likely to be regulated in the face of frustration and may have difficulty regulating other emotions.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the construct of temperament is multidimensional, and the dimensions of emotion regulation and physiological reactivity should be considered when examining temperament.
frustration in the early months of life may be an important indicator of later emotion regulation difficulties and physiological dysregulation.
the study of temperament in infancy should be extended beyond the assessment of reactivity to include the assessment of emotion regulation.
